newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Freed Russian hostages say held in Chechen cave.
newsitem.headline: Freed Russian hostages say held in Chechen cave.

text.p: A Russian television correspondent taken hostage in Chechnya and held with two colleagues for 100 days said on Tuesday they had been kept for most of the time in a mountain cave.

Yelena Masyuk, who won international awards for her bold coverage of the 21-month war between Chechen separatists and Russian troops, said they had often been tempted to pick up one of the guns lying near their captors, kill them and try to run.
"Thank God we had the strength not to do this," she told a news conference in Moscow a day after their release.
The three, freed after their commercial television company NTV paid what it said was a seven-figure dollar ransom, are among dozens of hostages taken around Chechnya since January.
Two Britons, five French people, a German, a Slovak and a Yugoslav are among those still being held.

NTV president Igor Malashenko accused the Chechen leadership of complicity in what he said was a lucrative business in trading captives, saying that even Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov must be aware of what was going on.
"All this is a big hostage-taking machine...under the direct leadership of Vice President Vakha Arsanov. Today we have no doubts about this," he said.

"We are sure that President Maskhadov, who visited Moscow yesterday, is at the very least aware of what is going on in his republic and...is either too weak and cannot help to free people or can and doesn't want to," he added.

Maskhadov has blamed shadowy external forces for the wave of captures, saying those masterminding them are intent on destabilising his war-ravaged republic, which is strategically placed across a key oil pipeline.
Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov, accused by Malashenko of masterminding a propaganda campaign to cover the hostage trade, said the NTV chief's statement was "idiotic".
"We hope that in time, he will calm down and understand that in making these statements he was, to put it mildly, not quite right," Udugov said in an inteview with Ekho Moskvy radio.

Masyuk said she and her team had at first been put in a basement, with just bread and tea to drink and a bucket for a toilet. "The worst was not the physical discomfort but being kept in the dark about what would happen to us," she said.
They were soon transferred to a cave. "The last two and a half months we spent in another cave," she said, adding it was 4,000 metres (13,000 feet) up in the Caucasus mountains of southern Chechnya.
She had been scared at times that their captors would kill them: "But I calmed myself with the fact that we were too valuable to them."

Malashenko, who has close links to the Kremlin, urged President Boris Yeltsin to take measures to stop the hostage trade. Yeltsin met Maskhadov on Monday and agreed to work on settling relations between Russia and its breakaway republic.
"The Russian state...turned out to be unable to protect its citizens and unable to free its citizens on the territory of the Russian Federation," he said.
During the conflict, which ended last August after tens of thousands had been killed and many more made homeless, Masyuk pulled no punches regarding Moscow's role in the carnage.

Many Russian journalists backed Yeltsin's ill-fated campaign against the separatists or tempered their criticism of the overwhemling force employed by Russian troops, tanks and aircraft in the tiny and mostly rural North Caucasus region.

Asked if her ordeal had changed her views, Masyuk said she had just been doing her job reporting what the war meant for the civilians who made up most of the casualties. She called her captors "monsters" but said she did not hate the Chechen people.
